title: REST & API Design Basics
summary: REST's actual constraints — resources, uniform interface, statelessness — plus versioning, pagination, and the RPC-vs-REST confusion interviewers probe.

slides.markdown:
**REST** (REpresentational State Transfer) is a set of architectural constraints, not a protocol or a format. The core idea: everything is a **resource** (a user, an order, a comment), each resource has a **representation** (usually JSON), and you interact with all of them through one **uniform interface** — the same handful of HTTP methods, applied consistently.

That uniformity is the actual value: once you know the pattern, you can guess how to interact with a resource you've never seen before, in an API you've never used.

URLs name **things** (nouns), not **actions** (verbs): `/orders/42` is resource-oriented; `/getOrder?id=42` is not. Nesting expresses relationships: `/users/7/orders` means "orders belonging to user 7."

The verb — what you're *doing* to that resource — comes from the HTTP method, not the URL. `DELETE /orders/42` reads naturally; `/deleteOrder/42` duplicates the same meaning in two places.

Create, Read, Update, Delete map cleanly onto HTTP methods and a resource collection/item URL pattern: `POST /orders` creates, `GET /orders/42` reads one, `PUT`/`PATCH /orders/42` updates, `DELETE /orders/42` removes.

Getting this mapping right is exactly what makes an API *predictable* — a client can guess the update endpoint for a resource it's never touched, purely from the pattern. See [HTTP Fundamentals](http-fundamentals) for the method/idempotency details.

slides.sectionTitle: Statelessness in REST vs stateful RPC
slides.markdown:
REST inherits HTTP's statelessness by design: every request carries everything needed to process it (auth token, parameters) — the server holds no per-client session between calls. A stateful RPC session, by contrast, might require calling `login()` first and keeping server-side session context for subsequent calls.

Statelessness is what makes REST APIs trivially horizontally scalable: any server behind a load balancer can handle any request, since none of them are holding client-specific state.

A well-designed REST API treats status codes as part of the contract, not an afterthought: `201 Created` (with a `Location` header) after a successful `POST`, `204 No Content` after a `DELETE` with nothing to return, `404` for a missing resource, `422 Unprocessable Entity` for validation failures versus `400` for malformed requests.

Getting this right means a generic HTTP client library — retry logic, caching, error handling — behaves correctly against your API without any custom parsing of the body.

| Approach | Example | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| URL path | `/v2/orders` | Most visible/cacheable, but "pollutes" the resource URL |
| Header | `Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json` | Cleaner URLs, harder to test/debug by hand |
| Query param | `/orders?version=2` | Easy to add, easy to forget/misuse |

URL-path versioning wins in practice for most public APIs precisely because it's the most discoverable and debuggable, even though it's architecturally less "pure."

Real collections need conventions beyond plain `GET /orders`: `?page=2&limit=50` or cursor-based `?after=<id>` for pagination, `?status=shipped` for filtering, `?sort=-created_at` for sorting (with a leading `-` meaning descending).

Cursor-based pagination is generally preferred over page-number pagination for large or frequently-changing datasets — page numbers can skip or duplicate rows if data is inserted between requests.

**HATEOAS** (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) is REST's most theoretically "pure" constraint: responses include links to related actions/resources, so a client discovers what it can do next from the response itself, rather than hardcoding URLs.

In practice, almost no production APIs implement it fully — clients are usually built against fixed documentation instead, since hypermedia-driven clients are significantly more complex to build for marginal real-world benefit.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: REST vs RPC vs GraphQL
slides.markdown:
| | REST | RPC-style | GraphQL |
|---|---|---|
| Mental model | Resources + uniform methods | Named remote functions | One query language, client picks fields |
| URL shape | `/orders/42` | `/getOrderDetails` | Single `/graphql` endpoint |
| Best fit | General CRUD APIs | Actions that don't map to resources well | Flexible, client-driven data needs |

(See also [system design: REST API design](rest-api-design) for the full trade-off discussion beyond this network-layer view.)

**Wrong belief:** "My API returns JSON over HTTP, so it's a REST API."

**Why it's wrong:** REST is defined by its constraints — resource orientation, a uniform interface, statelessness — not by the wire format. An API with `/api?action=getUser&id=5` returning JSON is just RPC-over-HTTP wearing REST's clothes; the URL isn't resource-oriented and the "verb" is smuggled into a query param.

**Correct model:** "RESTful" describes an architecture, not a content-type. Plenty of production APIs are honestly RPC-style and that's fine — the problem is only in mislabeling them.
